generator_view.scenario: You have taken photos only with a phone for years, but indoor volleyball images often look blurred or noisy. You have about 700 dollars for a first dedicated camera and are tempted to choose between an older interchangeable-lens model with a larger sensor and a newer compact with a smaller sensor. Treat that budget and your phone symptoms as anchors rather than measured results. The frozen shopping set contains an Olympus E-M1 body page at 668 dollars, a Panasonic ZS70 fixed-zoom bundle at 379.08 dollars, a Panasonic LX10 one-inch fixed-lens bundle at 514.87 dollars, a Canon 80D body page at 798 dollars, a Micro Four Thirds 35-100mm f/2.8 lens page at 897.99 dollars and a Canon-compatible 50-100mm f/1.8 lens page at 999 dollars. Frozen model context places the E-M1 in 2013 with a Four Thirds sensor and interchangeable mount, the LX10 in 2016 with a 13.2 by 8.8mm sensor and fixed 24-72mm-equivalent f/1.4-f/2.8 lens, the 80D in 2016 as a DSLR, and the ZS70 row in 2017 with a 1/2.3-type sensor and fixed 24-720mm-equivalent f/3.3-f/6.4 lens. Background material covers sensor format, aperture, exposure time, motion blur, image noise, autofocus and sports-photography equipment. Three community pages contain only scoped questions or author reports about dark-condition settings and phone noise, focus or oversharpening. No source supplies a controlled same-gym comparison, verified current condition and delivered cost, a complete compatible system under 700 dollars, or a universal sensor-size or release-year winner.

One MachineLearning author asks how ISO, f-number and exposure time affect a dark-condition dataset. Shutter speed is exposure time, and shorter exposure admits less light while helping limit motion blur from a moving subject. Lower f-numbers mean larger relative apertures and more entering light. Image noise can arise from sensor and electronic processes, and low-light capture trades exposure time, aperture and gain after their practical limits. Sensor format affects angle of view and can affect total light under matched comparison conditions, but the result is not a one-variable ranking. Stabilization can address camera shake but does not by itself freeze a volleyball player.
